This excerpt from Cory Doctorow's *Little Brother* (distributed free under Creative Commons license) introduces both the novel and its accompanying materials. Written in 2007 out of urgent concern about government surveillance and digital privacy loss, the work serves as both fiction and a call to action, encouraging readers to build technologies, engage with its themes, and resist censorship. Doctorow explains his philosophy on free distribution, arguing that sharing ebooks benefits rather than harms authors. The section includes a donation program encouraging purchases for classrooms and libraries, a dedication to Alice, and endorsements from prominent authors praising the novel as a timely, politically important story about teenage rebellion against surveillance through hacking and digital activism. Each chapter is dedicated to independent bookstores, promoting support for these establishments as venues for purchasing the paper edition.

He and his friend Darryl then attempt to evade the school's pervasive surveillance systems—which include gait-recognition cameras and RFID tracking via library books—to pursue clues in an alternate reality game. Marcus employs various countermeasures including hidden programs, TOR routing, gravel in his shoes, and a Faraday pouch to block RFID signals, exploiting gaps in the school's monitoring infrastructure.

# Combined Summary

Following a terrorist attack at San Francisco's Powell Street BART station, seventeen-year-old Marcus and his friends are abducted by Department of Homeland Security agents in an unmarked military-style vehicle and transported to a mobile command center. Shackled and hooded, Marcus is interrogated by armed agents who threaten him as a potential enemy combatant and demand he unlock his phone and decrypt its files. Despite escalating intimidation—including threats of disappearing into "dark holes"—Marcus repeatedly asserts his constitutional rights, refuses to unlock his phone citing his right to privacy, and demands legal representation. Though the agents employ aggressive tactics, claiming "honest people don't have nothing to hide," Marcus maintains his refusal, though he later reflects he may have made a mistake in not cooperating.

Marcus, a seventeen-year-old high school student, is illegally detained by the government following a terrorist attack on a Bay Area bridge and transported to a former military prison facility. There, a severe female agent systematically interrogates him, extracting his passwords and personal data by offering privileges in exchange for cooperation. Using psychological manipulation—including threats about treason and the death penalty—the agent coerces Marcus into signing documents falsely declaring his detention was voluntary and accuses him of involvement in placing bombs on the bridge, which he vehemently denies. Broken and desperate to escape, Marcus eventually complies with all demands. After being hooded and transported by ship, he is finally released in an alley near his city. Traumatized and expecting recapture, he cautiously makes his way to the sidewalk where he is embraced by someone waiting for him, finally realizing he is free.

After being detained for six days following terrorist attacks on the Bay Bridge and BART, the protagonist reunites with friends Vanessa and Jolu in North Beach to share their experiences of interrogation and imprisonment. Learning that their friend Darryl has disappeared and realizing he was singled out for refusing to unlock his phone, he convinces his friends to keep their capture secret and tell their parents they were quarantined in Oakland refugee camps. Upon arriving home, he maintains this fabricated story despite his parents revealing the attacks killed thousands and destroyed the BART tunnel.

Discovering a keystroke-logging bug planted by the Department of Homeland Security in his laptop, the protagonist becomes paranoid about surveillance. Unable to sleep, he retrieves a sealed Xbox Universal from his closet and installs ParanoidLinux, a government-resistant operating system designed for dissidents that encrypts communications and disguises covert activity. Accessing the secure system through his neighbors' wireless internet, he feels empowered by technology that protects rather than surveils him and resolves to convince his friends to adopt the same system.
